newsitem.title: USA: U.S. August output up but little inflation seen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. August output up but little inflation seen.

text.p: The nation's mines, factories and utilities boosted their output for a fifth month in a row during August, the Federal Reserve said Tuesday, but there were few signs of developing price pressures.
Total industrial output rose 0.5 percent after a 0.1 percent July gain, largely because of a surge in electricity output to meet summer cooling needs and more production by mining companies.
As a result, businesses operated at 83.5 percent of their maximum capacity last month, up from 83.3 percent in July.

Analysts said the report showed a healthy industrial sector, but with bountiful production capacity and signs of slowing in sectors like automaking that were consistent with a weaker pace of second-half economic expansion.
"Manufacturing is on the rise but its growth rate is sedate and is not enough to put pressure on capacity use," said Robert Dederick, economic consultant to Northern Trust Co. in Chicago.
For a second straight month, manufacturing companies operated at reduced capacity rates in August, down to 82.3 percent from 82.4 percent in July and 82.5 percent in June.

"We're actually seeing some ebbing of inflation pressures in the manufacturing sector," Dederick noted, which will be welcomed by the Fed when its policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee meets to plot interest-rate strategy next Tuesday.
But he said the Fed may be swayed by reports of rising wages and tight labour markets, possibly deciding to hike interest rates to quell inflationary potential there.

A senior Fed official said Tuesday that eight of the 12 district banks in the Federal Reserve System have requested a hike in the discount rate amid evidence that the pace of economic expansion was likely to remain brisk in the second half of the year.

The discount rate, at which the Fed lends funds to member banks, is now at 5 percent. The rate serves as a benchmark for loan rates in general. An increase would likely prompt banks to raise the prime rates they charge their best customers, affecting everything from credit card rates to auto loans.
Dederick said he expected third-quarter growth to ease to a 2.6 percent annual rate from a booming 4.8 percent in the second quarter.

A separate report from the American Bankers Association showed debt-laden consumers already were having difficulty in maintaining spending as late payments on credit cards hit a record high in the second quarter.
The bankers' group said 3.66 percent of all active credit-card accounts between April and June had delinquent payments, up from 3.53 percent in the first quarter.

That is expected to put the brakes on consumer spending. There were signs that was occurring as a retail sales report showed business down in the first two weeks of September when measured against August.
The Lynch, Jones and Ryan Inc. Redbook sales report eased 0.1 percent in the first two weeks of this month from August and many stores said the pace of sales activity was weaker than they expected.
Consumer spending fuels about two-thirds of national economic activity, so waning demand can quickly curb business' production plans.

During each of July and August, output by manufacturing companies went up a modest 0.3 percent. By contrast, utility companies' production jumped 1.5 percent in August after falling 1.8 percent in both June and July.
Mining output was up 2.4 percent after a 1 percent drop in July.

The rate of motor vehicle assemblies slowed in August after a July pickup. The assembly rate for new cars was down to an annual rate of 6.7 million from seven million in July and for light trucks it eased to 5.6 million last month from six million in July.

David Orr, economist for First Union Corp. in Charlotte, N.C., said growth in manufacturing in July and August was only about half the pace registered in May and June and was consistent with a moderating pace of national economic growth.
"The Fed was looking for a slowdown and it happened," Orr said, "The Fed may raise interest rates, but it shouldn't use this report as a rationale."
